summary: Describes a keyed MD5 transform for use with the IP Authentication Header, based on HMAC-MD5, with an option to guard against replay attacks.

eli5.summary: Each packet gets a secret seal, and a counter so that an old packet cannot be sent a second time.

questions: how to prevent replay attacks in ip authentication header
how does ah prevent replay attacks
what key length does hmac-md5 ah need
subtitle: A keyed MD5 transform for the IP Authentication Header, with an optional counter against replayed packets.

tldr.problem: The IP Authentication Header needs a concrete algorithm to produce authentication data, and a way to stop an attacker from storing a packet and sending it again later.
tldr.mechanism: The authentication data is HMAC-MD5 computed over the whole IP datagram with a shared secret key, and an optional 64-bit Replay Prevention counter, starting at 1, is included in the calculation.
tldr.outcome: Implementations claiming conformance with the IP Authentication Header (RFC 1826) MUST implement this transform. Its security rests on the strength of MD5, the key and the implementations.

today: The record lists RFC 2085 as a Proposed Standard, and no obsoleting or updating RFC is recorded for it. The text builds on RFC 1826 and RFC 2104.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Authentication Header (AH) of RFC 1826 provides integrity and authentication for IP datagrams. This RFC specifies a keyed-MD5 transform for it, based on HMAC-MD5. MD5 is a key-less hash function that produces a message digest. Combined with an AH Key, it yields authentication data, which is placed in the Authentication Data field and is also the basis of the data integrity service.

For protection against replay attacks, a Replay Prevention field is included as a transform option. The Security Parameters Index (SPI) is used to determine whether this option is included in the AH.

All implementations that claim conformance with the IP Authentication Header specification MUST implement this HMAC-MD5 transform.
sections.eli5: The packet's seal is made by mixing a secret with the packet's contents. A counter is an optional extra to catch copied packets.

sections.title: Keys and Data Size
sections.content:
The AH Key is a shared secret between two communicating parties. It is not a cryptographic key in the traditional sense: it is hashed with the transmitted data so that an intervening party cannot duplicate the authentication data. Even so, the usual concerns about keys apply. Keys need to be chosen at random, or generated with a cryptographically strong pseudo-random generator seeded with a random seed, and implementations should change the key as frequently as possible.

Implementations MUST support a key length of 128 bits or less and SHOULD support longer ones. The advice is to use the hash output length, 128 bits for MD5. A key length of zero is prohibited and MUST be prevented. Keys shorter than 128 bits are strongly discouraged. MD5 works on 64-byte blocks, so keys longer than 64 bytes are first hashed with MD5.

MD5 produces a 128-bit value, used as the authentication data. It is naturally 64 bit aligned, so no padding is needed for machines with native double words.
sections.eli5: The secret has to be hard to guess and not empty. A longer secret is fine, but a very short one is weak.

sections.title: The Packet Format
sections.content:
The header carries a Next Header field, a Length field, a RESERVED field, the SPI, the Replay Prevention field and the Authentication Data. Next Header, RESERVED and SPI are specified in RFC 1826. The Length field is the length of the Replay Prevention field and the Authentication Data in 32-bit words.

If Replay Prevention is not in use for the Security Association, the Authentication Data field directly follows the SPI field.
sections.eli5: The header is a label with the packet's type, its size, which secret deal it belongs to, the counter and finally the seal itself.

sections.title: Computing the Authentication Data
sections.content:
The authentication data is the output of MD5, calculated over the entire IP datagram. Fields that vary in transit, and the authentication data field itself, must contain all zeros before the computation. The Replay Prevention field, if present, is included.

With K as the shared key (hashed with MD5 first if longer than 64 bytes) and text as the data, two fixed strings are defined: ipad is the byte 0x36 repeated 64 times and opad is the byte 0x5C repeated 64 times. The result is MD5(K XOR opad, MD5(K XOR ipad, text)).

In steps: pad K with zeros to 64 bytes, XOR with ipad, append the text, apply MD5, XOR the padded K with opad, append the MD5 result, and apply MD5 again. Implementers are pointed to RFC 2104 for more detail, example code and performance improvements.
sections.eli5: The secret is mixed with the packet and scrambled once, then mixed with a different pattern and scrambled again. The final scramble is the seal.

sections.title: Replay Prevention
sections.content:
The Replay Prevention field is a 64-bit value that guarantees each packet exchanged between two parties is different. Each IPsec Security Association specifies whether it is used. The field is an up counter starting at a value of 1, and the shared key must not be used long enough for the counter to wrap, that is, to send more than 2^64 packets with one key.

On receipt the value is assured to be increasing. An implementation may accept out-of-order packets within a window whose size is an implementation detail, but it must ensure that any packet accepted out of order has not arrived before, so each packet is accepted at most once.

When the destination is a multicast address and several senders share the same Security Association, replay protection SHOULD NOT be enabled. For replay protection in that case, each sender SHOULD have its own Security Association.
sections.eli5: Every packet gets the next number on a ticket. If an old ticket number shows up again, it is turned away. With many senders sharing one ticket roll, the numbers get muddled, so each sender should have its own roll.

sections.title: Strength and Limits
sections.content: The security of this transform depends on the strength of MD5, the correctness of the algorithm's implementation, the security of the key management mechanism, the strength of the secret key, and the correctness of the implementations in all participating systems. The RFC refers readers to RFC 2104 for a detailed discussion of the strengths and weaknesses of MD5.
sections.eli5: A lock is only as good as the lock itself, the key and everyone using it properly.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of Replay Prevention and Authentication Data in 32-bit words.

fields.name: Replay Prevention
fields.desc: Up counter starting at 1; optional per Security Association.
